title: The Future Is Unknown, So Plan Accordingly | Dimensional
gist: Wes Crill of Dimensional argues that because market prices already embed the aggregate forecast of all investors, allocating on a personal forecast is a concentrated bet whose payoff distribution is far wider than most investors realize; his hard evidence is that over 2006-2025 the average yearly gap between the best- and worst-performing developed market countries exceeded 50 percentage points. The piece is short and promotional in structure (body plus a large disclosure block), so the actionable content is a single 'plan, don't predict' framework anchored to one country-dispersion data point.

insights.claim: Market prices are themselves already a forecast of the future because they are set in part by the aggregate of all investors' expectations about which companies will succeed, which economies will grow, and which markets will take off.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Treat any active tilt as a bet against an embedded consensus forecast rather than as a standalone view; the hurdle is being right where the market is wrong, not merely being right.
insights.quote: Markets set prices based in part on the aggregate of these expectations. So, market prices already represent a forecast of the future.
insights.locator: We all have views about what the future may bring

insights.claim: Allowing personal forecasts to drive asset allocation produces concentrated positions that fall short whenever the realized future differs from the prediction, making forecast-driven allocation a fragility rather than an edge.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Audit portfolios for concentration that exists only because of a macro or thematic call, and size those positions to survive being wrong.
insights.quote: Dogmatic adherence to forecasts dictates concentrated investments that fall short in the event the future differs from our predictions.
insights.locator: However, some investors may let their personal forecasts

insights.claim: Diversifying a portfolio is best understood not as a return-enhancing decision but as an explicit admission that the investor has no crystal ball, whose payoff is a narrower distribution of possible outcomes.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Judge diversification decisions on dispersion of outcomes rather than expected return, which reframes the cost of broad exposure as insurance premium rather than forgone alpha.
insights.quote: Diversifying portfolios is a tacit admission that we don’t have a crystal ball. You reduce the range of outcomes by preparing for what you can’t see coming.
insights.locator: Diversifying portfolios is a tacit admission

insights.claim: The operating principle advocated is 'plan, don't predict' — building a portfolio prepared for all possible outcomes instead of optimizing it around one specific forecast.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: A robustness-first mandate implies rebalancing rules and broad exposure over conviction sizing, and it is the framing an advisor should expect from a Dimensional-aligned allocation.
insights.quote: This echoes what we often say at Dimensional: Plan, don’t predict.
insights.locator: Rather than focusing on one specific forecast

insights.claim: Over the two decades from 2006 through 2025, the average yearly difference between the best-performing and worst-performing developed market country was more than 50 percentage points.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Quantifies the payoff spread on a single-country bet: a concentrated country call is roughly a coin flip on a 50-plus point annual swing, which should govern position sizing on any single-country ETF exposure.
insights.quote: The average difference between the best- and worst-performing developed market countries over the past two decades was over 50 percentage points.
insights.locator: Country stock market returns are a good example

insights.claim: Going all-in on one country's equity market because of a view on where its stocks are headed deliberately widens the investor's range of outcomes, with the upside of looking like a hero and the symmetric downside of a large miss.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Single-country concentration is a volatility decision as much as a return decision; watch for portfolios where a home-country or single-market tilt is unpriced risk rather than a deliberate bet.
insights.quote: Get your call right, and you’ll look like a hero. Get it wrong, and you’ll be as apoplectic as when Chevy Chase’s character loses the rock paper scissors game in Vegas Vacation.

insights.claim: A quarter-century-old Pentagon episode, reported in a recent Forbes article, saw the US military change how it identifies future threats after reviewing how quickly the geopolitical landscape evolves — concluding that preparing for all possible outcomes beat focusing on one specific forecast.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Supplies a non-financial precedent for scenario-preparedness over point forecasting, useful in client conversations where geopolitical narratives are driving concentration requests.
insights.quote: The change stemmed from a review of how quickly the geopolitical landscape evolves—yesterday’s adversaries can become tomorrow’s allies.
insights.locator: I saw a great Forbes article recently

insights.claim: The speed at which alliances invert — yesterday's adversaries becoming tomorrow's allies — is offered as the general reason forecast horizons decay, implying geopolitical-narrative-driven portfolio bets have short shelf lives.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Second-order read: positions built on a durable geopolitical alignment thesis should carry an explicit reassessment trigger, because the underlying alignment can flip faster than the holding period.
insights.locator: The change stemmed from a review
